transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-09
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Peregrine Head of ML), Raj Mehta (Peregrine Infra), Sofia Alvarez (Peregrine CTO)

Summary:
High-level deep dive into GPU runtime profiling for Peregrine's LLM inference workload. Focus areas: kernel selection behavior, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM tradeoffs, CUDA graphs to reduce kernel-launch overhead, KV cache semantics across requests, batching strategies, quantization options, and VPC/on-prem deployment constraints (KMS, SOC2). Agreed to run targeted CUDA-graph + TensorRT-LLM profiling with Peregrine sample prompts; Redwood to share benchmark template and initial recommendations.

Topics covered:
- Kernel selection and fused kernels (convolution/fused attention)
- TensorRT-LLM performance characteristics vs vLLM (memory layout, batching)
- CUDA graphs for steady-state generation and kernel launch overhead reduction
- KV cache persistence and eviction during multi-tenant on-prem runs
- Batching strategy: dynamic vs fixed, effect on p50/p95 latency and throughput
- Quantization impact (FP16, INT8, per-channel vs per-tensor) and accuracy tradeoffs
- VPC/on-prem considerations: KMS/HSM, audit logs, rolling upgrades

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone thanks for joining, um today Maya and I want to dig into the runtime profiling you sent and go over kernel selection + trt-llm vs vllm and, uh, how cuda graphs might help you with your latency SLOs.
[00:18] Lena: thanks, yeah we saw some of the numbers you sent, curious why p95 spikes at 800ms even when p50 is 120ms. we've got fairly tight SLOs for real time assistants.
[00:32] Maya: right, so quick context, trt-llm uses a lot of fused kernels and custom kernel scheduling which minimizes ops and memory copies, whereas vllm is more CPU-friendly and uses persistent CUDA kernels but has different batching semantics. for some workloads trt-llm gives better tokens/sec but can be less flexible for dynamic batch sizes.
[00:55] Raj: can you expand on fused kernels? we saw mention of cuBLAS, cutlass, and then another layer in your notes. sometimes the model name gets garbled in our logs so not sure which kernels are running.
[01:08] Maya: sure. fused kernels here means attention + qkv + output fused into fewer kernels so you reduce global memory traffic. that helps latency, particularly at mid-sequence lengths. you will see a shift in kernel profile if your seq length or kv cache behavior changes.
[01:25] Samir: also important - kernel selection can be dynamic in our runtime, we pick different execution paths based on sequence length, batch size, and available memory. we log kernel IDs in the trace, but yes sometimes the probe names are a bit off in exported nvprof logs.
[01:40] Lena: that matches our experience, the first token is fast but after a few tokens things slow and we suspect re-warming the cache or evicting kv segments.
[01:50] Maya: that sounds like kv cache thrash, especially if you have many concurrent users with large context windows. on vLLM you sometimes see more predictable cache usage because it pins more memory per session; trt-llm may favor smaller per-request working sets but will recompile or switch kernels if shapes change.
[02:10] Raj: curious about cuda graphs, we've heard they reduce kernel launch overhead, but how much in practice?
[02:18] Maya: in our internal tests cuda graphs cut per-token CPU overhead by 40-70% in steady-state generation. the key is you need a steady shape (batch size + seq length) to capture in a graph. dynamic batching breaks graphs unless you use a small set of pre-captured graphs for each common shape.
[02:41] Samir: yep, for Peregrine we recommended capturing graphs for (bs=1,SL=512), (bs=4,SL=512) and maybe a few longer windows. the graph capture cost is one-time but you must manage fallbacks; our runtime will fallback to non-graph path when it sees a new shape.
[03:05] Sofia: what about model quantization? we can't lose more than 1-2% absolute quality on our NLU tasks. is INT8 safe?
[03:13] Maya: good question. int8 with calibration (per-channel quant) often gets you 2-3x speedup on kernels with tensor cores, but for some models you may see a quality delta. FP16 is the safer win: generally 1.5x throughput improvement with almost no quality loss. we recommend running evals with your prompt set; we'll help create an eval harness.
[03:33] Lena: okay so action items - we'll send the representative prompts. also we run on-prem in a VPC with KMS for key management, any special considerations?
[03:45] Samir: for private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM. also RBAC + audit logs are important for you — we can enable detailed kernel-level logging and tie it to SSO identities but that increases log volume.
[03:58] Raj: is there any perf hit from KMS calls on request path?
[04:02] Maya: no, keys are fetched at startup and the decryption is local — normal setup has negligible runtime hit. you might see slight bootstrap latency on container start or key rotation events.
[04:15] Lena: back to kernel selection — can you show an example trace?
[04:18] Maya: yeah I'll share a sample nvtx trace and a collapsed kernel timeline. we saw one case where the runtime switched from a fused attention kernel to a non-fused path due to an odd sequence length (like 37 tokens) which caused extra launches. small shape variation can trigger suboptimal kernels.
[04:40] Samir: that's why batching policies matter. if you use micro-batching to align shapes (pad to 64 or 128 multiples), you get more consistent kernel selection and better cuda-graph reuse. downside is added padding cost and memory.
[04:55] Raj: our mem is often tight; would quantization then help the padding overhead?
[04:59] Maya: yes, quantization reduces memory footprint, so you can afford more padding/batching. plus int8 often reduces GPU memory allowing larger effective batch sizes. note though that quantized kernels sometimes have different fusion opportunities.
[05:15] Lena: metrics to capture for our next run?
[05:18] Maya: p50/p95/p99 latency per prompt type, tokens/sec throughput, GPU utilization, GPU memory usage, kernel launch counts, average kernel time, and kv cache hit/miss rates. also trace nvtx ranges for graph vs non-graph paths.
[05:33] Samir: we'll add sequence-length distribution and request concurrency to the spreadsheet.
[05:37] Raj: about vLLM vs TensorRT-LLM — which should we prefer for Peregrine?
[05:44] Maya: tradeoffs: if you need flexible dynamic batching and rapid model iteration, vLLM (or a CPU+GPU hybrid) can be easier. TRT-LLM shines when you can standardize shapes and want max throughput/lowest per-token cost on NVIDIA GPUs. if you have lots of long-context sessions and KV cache locality, TRT-LLM plus CUDA graphs and fused kernels tends to be better for steady-state throughput.
[06:08] Sofia: price is a consideration too — what's the engineering cost of maintaining graphs and multiple kernels?
[06:13] Samir: initial engineering time to capture graphs and set up fallbacks is non-trivial (a week or two for a single model), but after that maintenance is low: most changes are model-versioned and we keep a graph catalog per version. we can help manage that as part of Dedicated or Private deployments.
[06:30] Maya: quick note on kernel selection for quantized models: TensorRT will choose INT8-optimized kernels but sometimes falls back if calibration tables aren't available at runtime; we recommend pre-calibrating in CI.
[06:43] Lena: any gotchas for multi-tenant on-prem?
[06:46] Maya: yes: KV cache eviction and noisy neighbors. if you pack many small sessions on the same GPU, you have to tune allocator and eviction policies. Redwood offers per-tenant cgroups for memory allocation and we surface KV eviction stats in the Console.
[07:02] Raj: good to know.
[07:05] Samir: recap and next steps: we'll share a benchmark sheet, Maya will run a CUDA graph capture experiment against your sample model and return traces, Raj will provision short-lived access and send the prompts. then we'll reconvene after you see the initial graphs.
[07:22] Lena: perfect. thanks all.

End of meeting.
